wallet.name: apps/wallet
wallet.label: the owner's web app
wallet.desc: The web app the node's owner runs it from, built into the dassie binary. The owner's 20-word phrase is checked and turned into keys right in the browser, and never sent to the node.
does: Setup and login: a new phrase shown numbered as a metal plate holds it, and a phrase typed by its first four letters, with any correction shown word by word for the owner to confirm
Accounts and ledgers, sending and receiving, payment status and activity

Deposit pages like an exchange's: the address as a QR code, what to send, and the reserve; a button for testnet XRP from the faucet, and none on mainnet, which has no faucet; for a dollar token, DSUSD on the testnet or RLUSD on mainnet, both the token and the XRP its fees need, at the same address, and that DSUSD is bought with XRP on the testnet's pool
A dollar token's ledger shows its peg guard: the token's last price on its pool, and while the node pauses it, why: off its peg, or its price unread
A page of what the node holds outside its books, as the ledger reports it: its XRP and reserve, its token lines, and whether an issuer froze one

A page of each settlement hub the node is in, drawn in Kopje: its balance, the holds toward each peer and from it, the move on its way, depositing and withdrawing, since when a token's issuer froze the hub, and the hub's payout once it ended or stalled
Wallet addresses and payment requests for Open Payments
The consent page for apps, the apps it has let in, and their grants

The network as the node routes over it, its peers online and offline, bans, and the node's settings; a peer's details list each settlement method with what is owed on it, and a ledger being removed says the node is settling up with its peers first
Names for the node: registering one, how it stands with each registrar, and renewing it
The owner's sessions and paired devices, and on the node's own machine a QR code that pairs a new app
Debug pages, and live data over RPC streams, asked for again every few seconds where no stream carries it yet

dashboard.name: apps/dev-dashboard
dashboard.label: dev network dashboard
dashboard.desc: The dashboard of the local development network. It shows every node at once and opens any node's debug pages.
does: Pick or switch a scenario, add a node
A graph of all nodes and their peerings
The logs of the dev server and every node, merged
Each node's pages, reached through a relay to its IPC socket

website.name: apps/website
website.label: dassie.land
website.desc: This website, in Kopje, the visual identity: static pages built by Vite and published from main to a bucket behind the release mirror's load balancer, under a strict content security policy.
does: The home page, the Quick Start and the NixOS guide
This architecture page, drawn from one data file
The brand page: Kopje, the visual identity, with the mark, color, type and how they look in use
The STREAM toy: Dassie's own STREAM code, compiled to WebAssembly, sends a payment over a simulated network
Its packet log decrypts every STREAM packet

ui.name: packages/ui
ui.label: shared Solid UI
ui.desc: The building blocks the wallet, the dev dashboard and the STREAM toy share.
does: Amounts in any currency
A log viewer with filters
The network graph and its layout
Debug pages, the router and the theme, and Kopje's palette for a page that draws in it
Live data: RPC snapshots and changes, turned into Solid signals and stores

rpc.name: packages/rpc
rpc.label: RPC client
rpc.desc: The TypeScript client for the node's RPC contract, generated from the protobuf files. A test fails if the generated code is stale.
does: Over a WebSocket in browsers
Over the node's IPC socket in Node
Cancels calls and streams, and follows a reconnect

wasm.name: packages/wasm
wasm.label: Rust cores in WebAssembly
wasm.desc: The Rust core crates compiled to WebAssembly, with TypeScript bindings: one build for browsers and Node, in two modules, so the wallet loads identity without STREAM. The wallet derives keys with exactly the code the node runs.
does: Identity: phrase to node key, node ID and login proof
ILP packets and STREAM, for the STREAM toy and the interop tests
Decrypting STREAM packets, for the STREAM toy
Phrases made, and read with corrections the owner confirms
The phrase of a given secret, for the dev network's nodes

wasm-crate.name: dassie-wasm
wasm-crate.label: the core crates' JavaScript bindings
wasm-crate.desc: The wasm-bindgen bindings of the core crates, in a crate of their own, so the core crates know nothing of JavaScript. It is also where the browser's randomness comes in; the core crates only take an injected generator.
does: Identity, as one module
STREAM with ILP's packet codecs, as another
Times, amounts and packets checked at the edge, as JavaScript hands them over

apps-dev.name: apps/dev
apps-dev.label: local dev network
apps-dev.desc: `node --run dev`: a network of real dassie nodes on one machine, so development runs the same code that ships.
does: Builds the binary and the fake XRP Ledger, the only XRP Ledger its scenarios settle on, starts the nodes on `dN.localhost` and restarts them when the Rust code changes
An SNI proxy on port 443, local certificates, the dev nodes' identities, a rates server
Sets nodes up through their own RPC, the same way the end-to-end tests do

The scenario library, in which no node that runs settles directly: one node, two and six on the stub with unlimited trust, which never settles; DSUSD in an owner book, which the fake ledger's issuer mints; a node in the live realm holding XRP and RLUSD in owner books on the fake ledger's mainnet; `live-hub`: the live realm's hubs of XRP and RLUSD on the fake ledger's mainnet, every account funded by a deposit; a settlement hub on the fake ledger with four validators and two members; payments across currencies, converted between the stub and such a hub by a node in both; an XRP hub and a DSUSD hub with one member in each alone and two in both; and a market maker's, one or two core nodes in both hubs with its two periphery nodes, one in each hub, pinned to each

Founds a scenario's hubs through their sponsor's own RPC, a DSUSD hub with terms that name the token, with a validator file for each of its validators, and has its members join each with the founded hub's rules and fund their accounts in it from their own XRP or DSUSD
Drives the fake ledger as a scenario or a test asks: its issuer mints, freezes and claws back, its pool is set, and XRP arrives from outside

Runs the live realm only by the node's dev switch and only against the fake ledger's mainnet, funding each node's account by a deposit, as mainnet has no faucet; a live scenario's nodes start from scratch each run, since mainnet never resets

e2e.name: tests/e2e
e2e.label: real binaries
e2e.desc: End-to-end tests that run the real dassie binary, with real sockets. They check the IO layer the simulations replace.
does: A fresh install through `dassie init` and browser setup, with Pebble as the certificate authority
BTP payments, and the two-node and six-node scenarios routing across hops on the stub with unlimited trust, which never settles
Open Payments, including a third party's full flow with consent in the wallet

A settlement hub founded on the fake XRP Ledger: the faucet funds its members' own XRP, from which they fund their accounts in the hub, peer and settle over it alone, and keep their books across restarts; the wallet shows a member where to deposit
DSUSD in an owner book on the XRP Ledger: the issuer's mint booked, the peg guard pausing its conversions while still booking what arrives, and the issuer freezing the line and clawing back

Payments across currencies: dollars on the stub with unlimited trust, converted by a node in both and paid in XRP over a settlement hub, which the converter settles over; and across two hubs, of XRP and of DSUSD: a payment from a member of the XRP hub alone to a receiver in DSUSD of a member of the DSUSD hub alone, through a member of both that converts

Mainnet's schemes in the live realm, by the dev switch, on the fake ledger's mainnet: a node holds XRP and RLUSD in owner books on one account, at addresses under `g.`, and books a deposit once, across a restart too; RLUSD pauses while its pool gives no price and runs again once it reads one, and pauses while the pool prices it off its peg, still booking what arrives
Mainnet hubs in the live realm: an XRP hub and an RLUSD hub founded on the fake ledger's mainnet, and their members paying each other over both

Passive rebalancing end to end, over an XRP hub and a DSUSD hub: a market maker trades through a core node short of dollars and swaps back through the fake ledger's pool, which moves the node toward balance and earns the market maker; with two such core nodes, it trades through each; until a core node prices each asset whole, its hub and its owner book together, it checks only that a trade crosses each core node over both hubs
The wallet, the dev dashboard and dassie.land in a browser
The installer and the updater on Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora and CentOS, in containers

interop.name: tests/interop
interop.label: vs. other code
interop.desc: Checks Dassie against independent implementations of the same standards.
does: dassie-stream, native and in WebAssembly, against the npm `ilp-protocol-stream`, both ways
Golden vectors through the WebAssembly build
The WebAssembly modules in a browser
A stopped peer still answers correctly

dsusd-keeper.name: apps/dsusd-keeper
dsusd-keeper.label: DSUSD pool keeper
dsusd-keeper.desc: Keeps DSUSD, a testnet dollar token of Dassie's own, in place on the XRP Ledger testnet, and holds its XRP/DSUSD pool at an exchange's XRP/USD price. Owners get DSUSD only by paying XRP for it through that pool. It runs every few minutes on a small VM of its own.
does: Reads the exchange's XRP/USD ticker, and refuses one that is stale, crossed or out of bounds
Makes the token's issuer, its own account, its trust line and the pool, again after a testnet reset, from the faucet
Moves the pool's price to the target with DSUSD alone: mints and deposits it to raise XRP's price, withdraws it and gives it back to the issuer to lower it; it never buys XRP
Deepens the pool with faucet XRP and DSUSD beside it, up to a configured depth
One line per run, and a VM set up by `provision.sh` that reads only the two seeds it needs

market-maker.name: apps/market-maker
market-maker.label: testnet market maker
market-maker.desc: Runs `dassie market-maker` on a small VM of its own, so that the testnet's core nodes are brought back toward balance. Its two periphery nodes run beside it, one a member of the testnet's XRP hub and one of its DSUSD hub, each pinned to every core node it trades through. It runs once the testnet's default hubs are built into a release, and moves its targets toward balance once a core node prices each asset whole, its hub and its owner book together.
does: `provision.sh` makes the VM, a network that nothing reaches, and an account that can read only the two nodes' passphrases
On its first boot, installs the newest release with `install.sh --no-service`, and at each boot the units from `main`

Sets each node up from its passphrase with `dassie setup`, joining the default hub of its asset with the owner books that fund it, then runs the market maker; the passphrases sit in files in memory only while it runs
Updates every day with `dassie update --unit`, which restarts the nodes on the new version and goes back if one does not start
Logs to the serial console, so it is watched without SSH

proto-owner.name: proto/dassie/owner/v1
proto-owner.label: the owner's RPC contract: calls and live streams
proto-owner.desc: The contract between a node and its owner's clients, written in protobuf. Rust and TypeScript are both generated from it, so a change starts here.
does: Config, TLS, certificates and sessions
Ledgers, with a dollar token's peg guard, BTP tokens, payments and debug data
The node's account in each settlement hub it is in, and since when a token's issuer froze the hub, and the owner's moves into it and out of it, naming the hub by its ID
Founding a settlement hub as its sponsor, and the payout bundles the node keeps of each of its hubs

Nodes, peers, routes, settlements and bans; every settlement method of a peering, each with its credit, what is owed, and whether it is withdrawn or being wound down, and for a ledger being removed how many methods are left to wind down
The owner's names: registering and renewing them, and how each stands with each registrar
Wallet addresses, payments, grants and Send, to a wallet, a payment request or STREAM credentials
`Subscribe*` streams: a snapshot, then changes, at most 4 a second
Carried over a WebSocket (browsers) or the IPC socket (the CLI and Node), at most 1 MiB a message

proto-dev.name: proto/dassie/dev/v1
proto-dev.label: the dev network's control channel
proto-dev.desc: The contract between the dev server and its dashboard: scenarios, nodes and logs. Everything stays on loopback, on one origin.
does: List and switch scenarios, add nodes, reset
Relays the dashboard to each node's IPC socket, so no node accepts a dev token

cli.name: dassie-cli
cli.label: the dassie binary
cli.desc: The binary a server runs, with the wallet built in. Everything a node owner runs is a subcommand of it, and so are a front door and a market maker.
does: `dassie daemon`: standalone, or socket-activated by systemd
`dassie init`: the domain name and the certificate, then a URL to finish setup in the browser

`dassie status`, which also says whether a core node's rate feed reaches anyone and lists each peer's settlement methods with their credit and what is owed, `dassie setup-url` to print that URL again, and `dassie pair` for a code that pairs an owner app

`dassie setup`: sets a node up without a browser, from its owner's passphrase in a file on the node's host, sets each XRP Ledger account's own config (`--asset`, its server and faucet), and adds the settlement schemes it lacks, then joins the realm's default settlement hub when the build has one: on the testnet unless `--no-hub`, and in the live realm only with `--hub`, since on mainnet a node joins a hub only once its owner turns hubs on; run again, it changes nothing, and it refuses a node that is another passphrase's

`dassie hub`: shows the node's account in each settlement hub it is in, and since when a token's issuer froze one, moves the owner's funds between one and the node's XRP Ledger account, turns the node's own moves on or off, and gives up a move the hub has not shown for long; `dassie hub found` founds a hub with validators the owner picks, on the XRP Ledger network of the node's realm, and `dassie hub payout` shows the payout bundles kept of a hub and, once a quorum signed one set, its transactions to submit
`dassie update`: fetches, verifies and switches to a newer release, and goes back if it does not start
`dassie verify-install`, which also names the release key

`dassie front-door`: runs a front door, which is no node, and serves names by reading the bootstrap nodes' name lists itself (`DASSIE_BOOTSTRAP_NODES`); `--make-key` makes its key and prints the entry a node names it by

`dassie market-maker`: watches the signed rate feeds of one or more core nodes and, with two nodes of its own that each keep an uplink to every one of them, pays through the core node whose rates leave the widest margin against an AMM pool on the XRP Ledger, after a quote confirms it; then swaps its funds back through the pool with a `SendMax` that bounds the price

node.name: dassie-node
node.label: the daemon: IO, TLS, RPC, the engine
node.desc: The only part that does IO. It wires the sans-IO cores below to sockets, the database and the clock. Every service is a supervised task that restarts with backoff if it fails.
does: The database and its migrations, HTTPS and IPC listeners, TLS and ACME, the owner's login
The engine: ledger, connector, BTP server and STREAM receiver

Runs only the ledgers of its realm, test or live; the live realm is refused where it is set, at start and as a ledger activates, unless a dev switch that only builds with debug assertions honour turns it on
The peer protocol over QUIC, its only transport, with each node's key pinned, and a short backoff from a node it cannot reach; the settlement loop

QUIC over a WebSocket where UDP is blocked: every node takes the same QUIC packets at `/quic` on its HTTPS listener, and a node without a URL dials there when UDP has not connected within a second, keeping whichever connection proves the key first; where the network sets an HTTP proxy, that dial goes through it

QUIC connections held apart by who opened them, as the key each proved says: core peers, downlinks and everyone else each have room of their own, so many downlinks never crowd out the links that carry the network

Relayed streams: any QUIC node relays for the nodes connected to it, with TLS end to end, so a node without a public address that keeps a connection to a relay is still reached for Open Payments and by the owner's paired apps; a node without a hostname keeps one to the `dassiepay.net` front door unless `DASSIE_RELAY` names another or, empty, none

Front doors: a server with a key of its own and a wildcard certificate that takes Open Payments requests for `<node ID>.<domain>` and passes them to the node the ID names, or for `<name>.<domain>` to the name's holder, which it takes from the registrars' name lists as every node does, over relayed streams it opens on the connection the node keeps to it; it returns only the node's signed JSON, under a policy that lets nothing run, and never a node's page or a cookie; at the root of a name it shows a short static page of its own, saying what the name is and whether the node is connected; on its relay host it takes QUIC over a WebSocket at `/quic` too, so a node whose UDP is blocked keeps it as its relay
RPC with live streams, the log ring, the database inspector, and a discovery document at `/.well-known/dassie/node` that names the node's ID, key and feed port

The owner's names, registered and renewed through the peer node, and how each stands with each registrar, streamed to the wallet; once the node holds a name, it accepts and signs Open Payments requests under `<name>.dassiepay.net` too, and under `<name>.<domain>` at any other front door its owner names it at, which front doors pass on to it, and stops when it no longer holds it
Owner apps paired by the owner on the node's own machine: each proves a device key on a relayed stream and calls the RPC as the owner until it is revoked

Open Payments over HTTPS and relayed streams: wallet addresses, incoming payments, the GNAP authorization server, quotes and outgoing payments, each answer signed with the node key and written under the name the request came through; as a client at `dassiepay.net`, and when it fetches a client's key set there, the node takes only answers signed by the node whose ID the host names, or by a name's holder in its own view
Exchange rates, fetched from several sources, the fee and spread on what passes between peers, and the price table rebuilt from them and the owner's funds whenever either changes

A core node's rate feed: the price table, signed once and sent over UDP to every subscriber that proved its address, at most once a second while it changes, with the feed's port in the node's discovery document and its link state, and its counters in the owner's status rather than the log
Credit to each peer over a settlement hub: the node's own hold toward the peer, kept in step as the hold is funded and taken from, and nothing beyond it

Settlement methods: a peering's accounts, credit, requests to settle and their backoff, and the credit over each hub kept per method, each on its own ledger, and every method stored with its peering; a further method is taken while its accounts fit; each packet takes a method by structure, the one of the ledger it came in on where the hop has it, so a method short of room answers T04 and never passes the packet to another; the owner's removal of a scheme that peers settle on is not refused but winds their methods on it down, the scheme running until each is dropped, across a restart too, and the owner sees every method of each peering

Peerings over a settlement hub: the node lists every hub it is a member of, one per asset, in its link state and peers over it with members of the same hub, sends a commitment with each Prepare and a claim with each reply to a Fulfill, and books what a peering cost beyond its hold as a loss on the peer; a node with no account in its hub is paid into it by a member it peers with: their packets go without promises until then, the books alone taking them, and the member pays it in with all it owes once that reaches the hub's minimum for a new account, never before

Settlement hubs' validator role, which an owner turns on for the sponsors it lists: a validator per hub, its consensus state and ledger written before each step's messages go out, the hub's messages over a QUIC stream of their own, and the hub's escrow followed on the XRP Ledger only through a verifier of the network's UNL, attesting only what it proved: deposits, outcomes and clawbacks by their transactions' proofs, the escrow's setup and the issuer's hold by state proofs at a fresh anchor, and resets of the test network; it hands the XRPL connection no escrow transaction while the issuer holds a token hub's escrow, and the connection holds back what it queued before, sends open withdrawals again until they settle, and loses no deposit a freeze left without room

Founding settlement hubs: as a sponsor, it asks the validators its owner picked to accept the terms, gathers a quorum's signatures of the genesis and hands them the certificate, then funds the escrow from its XRP Ledger account and sets it up; as a validator, it accepts only listed sponsors' terms, on the XRP Ledger network its owner names (the testnet unless it names another), within its bound on hubs, signs one genesis per nonce and runs the hub its certificate founds

A member's copies of each of its hubs' payout bundles, fetched from each validator once the hub ended or stalled, checked against the rules and kept, so the member can pay itself out if the validators are gone

Funding its account in each hub it is in, on its own, from the owner book of the hub's asset, its XRP Ledger account for the XRP hub: the node opens it with a first deposit, deposits when what it can spend falls below a floor of what its hub peerings need, and withdraws what goes above a ceiling, both counted in the largest packet; one move at a time, kept in the database until the hub account's counters show it, so a restart never pays one twice; nothing moves into or out of a frozen hub; the owner sees every hub and moves funds in one, and may turn the node's own moves off

Simulated as a network of real engine cores, in tests and by `dassie-sim`: each seed draws its nodes, faults and payments, on the stub with unlimited trust, settling on the stub with commitments, or, in a share of seeds, settling over a settlement hub of XRP run in the simulation, runs them through chaos, then heals the network, which must settle down; over a settlement hub run in the simulation, a member's connection to the fake XRP Ledger may come back to a server that lies, and every node's books must still hold to what the ledger and the hub really did; and nodes keep their owner's books on a fake XRP Ledger through an issuer's freezes and clawbacks and lying servers

wallet-assets.name: dassie-wallet-assets
wallet-assets.label: the wallet, built in
wallet-assets.desc: The wallet's built files, embedded at build time, which the dassie binary and the desktop app hand the daemon to serve. A crate of its own, so that a change to the wallet rebuilds this table and relinks the binaries, rather than compiling the node again.
does: Each file with its media type, an ETag from its content and, where it pays, a gzip copy
Only the wallet `DASSIE_WALLET_DIST` names; without it, the node's placeholder page, so building Dassie needs no Node.js

desktop.name: dassie-desktop
desktop.label: the node in a window
desktop.desc: The desktop app for Linux: the owner's node runs inside it as a periphery node, with no public IP or hostname, and its wallet opens in a window. A tray icon keeps the node running after the window closes.
does: Runs the daemon in its own process, with HTTPS on loopback and QUIC on every address, so it dials its relay and uplinks, and no HTTP listener or rate feed socket, which a periphery node on loopback never uses
Loads the wallet from the node's own `https://localhost` origin, and trusts exactly the certificate its node serves there
Opens links to public pages in the browser, and loads nothing else
Starts at login in the tray, unless its owner turns that off
`nix run .#desktop` runs it

release.name: release
release.label: installer & updater
release.desc: How Dassie ships: Nix builds static binaries for x64 and arm64 with the wallet inside, CI signs and publishes them to get.dassie.land, and systemd runs the node and updates it every day. On NixOS, a flake from the mirror runs the same binary.
does: Static musl binaries, deterministic bundles and the mirror tree, built by Nix
`SHA256SUMS`, signed with minisign; the signature names the version
A release for each version tag, checked by dassie-release before it is published
`install.sh`, and systemd units for the node, its sockets and the daily update
Installs, updates and uninstalls, tested on four Linux distributions
A flake for NixOS with each release: a module and the signed binary, without the updater, tested in a VM

xrpl.name: dassie-xrpl
xrpl.label: XRP Ledger settlement
xrpl.desc: The node's XRP Ledger accounts, on the testnet and on mainnet, and the schemes on them, each the owner's book of what the node holds there, which funds its settlement hubs: one in each network's XRP, and a token scheme in each network's dollar token, DSUSD, Dassie's own testnet dollar, and on mainnet RLUSD, Ripple's. None of them peers: peers settle only over hubs. Mainnet's books hold real money and run only in the live realm; the testnet's RLUSD scheme is disabled. Also the wallet, the transaction codec, the rippled API, the account that connects, signs and follows the ledger, and the schemes that book what the account tells them. It also prices the ledger's AMM pools and signs the Payments that swap through one, and reads what the validators sign: ledger headers, validations and manifests, and the branches that prove a transaction, a ledger object or an object's absence in a ledger; and the UNL, from the signed validator lists of the publishers each network trusts, with the quorum of it that validates a ledger. The account fetches those lists and anchors on ledgers its UNL validated, which alone tell it which ledgers are validated and whether the testnet was reset, and proves at each anchor all it reads: what it holds, its trust lines, their issuers and the pools, and each transaction it books, found by the history its proven state names. So it checks the validators itself, and takes no server's word. The same checks also stand alone, apart from any account of the node's, for a settlement hub's validators, which attest only what it proved of their escrow and its issuer: a verifier that keeps its own UNL and anchor and proves what any account, trust line or signer list holds, and whether a transaction applied. A fake ledger, the testnet or mainnet, serves the tests and the dev network, with each network's dollar from an issuer at its address and pools to swap through, and validators of its own that sign each ledger, so it proves what it holds as a patched rippled would, or lies on request.
does: Derives the node's XRP Ledger wallets from its key, one per network, so the same phrase finds the same funds
Keeps the testnet and mainnet apart: each network's account has its own keys, and refuses a server of the other, and each scheme its own ledger
Keeps one connection per account, and hands out its sequences so schemes on it never take the same one
Signs Payments byte for byte as `xrpl.js` does, and writes token Payments, TrustSets and Payments with a `SendMax` the same way
Writes what sets up an account several keys control, such as a settlement hub's escrow, and signs it with Ed25519 or secp256k1 keys, one key alone or several signers each alone, as `xrpl.js` does
Reads an AMM pool with `amm_info` and prices its swaps exactly, rounding to the pool as the ledger does, for a client that converts on the ledger
Reads token amounts exactly, and a trust line, its flags and its issuer from either side

Reads any of the ledger's binary records in their one canonical form, hashes ledger headers, and checks validators' signatures on ledgers and the manifests that name their keys, pinned by records captured from mainnet and the testnet

Checks a branch in a ledger's tree of transactions or of state, which proves a transaction with its metadata, a ledger object, or that a key is absent, pinned by a mainnet ledger's transaction tree rebuilt to its root

Verifies the validator lists that mainnet's two publishers and the testnet's sign, takes the validators' newer manifests, and combines the lists into a UNL as rippled's defaults do, whose quorum validates a ledger, pinned by the live lists and validations

Fetches each publisher's list through the node and keeps it, then anchors the account on a ledger its own UNL validated, with fresh signatures: only an anchor moves what it takes as validated, never an older one

Tells a testnet reset from a server behind by the skip lists of the ledgers it anchors on, and stops instead on mainnet, which never resets; stalls, saying why, when it has no list, no quorum, a server without proofs or one whose history is too short

Proves at each anchor what the account holds, its sequence, its trust lines, their issuers' freezes, the reserve and the pools its schemes read, with one state proof, and that the account is gone only by a proof of absence

Finds every transaction it books by the history its proven state names, from each object back to what it told, and proves each in a ledger of the anchor's chain; the server's history and stream only name them sooner

Proves, apart from any account of the node's, what any account's root, trust line or signer list holds at a ledger, and whether a transaction applied and in which ledger, against ledgers its own UNL validated, for a settlement hub's validators watching their escrow; for objects its holder names, it also reports the transaction that changed each before
Cancels a payment only once its absence is proven, by the account's sequence past its last ledger, or by the transaction that took its number
Books every validated transaction once: deposits, withdrawals, the owner's payments and fees
Pays out of the account, or a token's line, for the owner, with a destination tag and a memo, as a deposit into a settlement hub is made, and books it as the owner's withdrawal once validated
Runs every scheme as an owner book: it books what the node holds and pays for the owner, and peers with nobody, whatever its config says
Books a dollar token, DSUSD on the testnet or RLUSD on mainnet, on a trust line it sets up itself, in dollars by what reaches the line, the issuer's clawbacks included
Pays a token scheme's fees in XRP: booked on the XRP ledger when the XRP scheme shares the account, off the books otherwise
Pays nothing out of a line the issuer froze, and says when the line cannot receive
Stops the node's conversions to and from a dollar token's ledger and its settlement hub's while the token's AMM pool, priced at the node's XRP rate, says it is off its dollar peg or cannot be read

Never books the reserve, and catches up after a restart from what the account and each scheme keep, each in one versioned encoding that a reader of another version refuses, but for a scheme's layout before its own, which it reads and keeps what an owner book needs of
Asks the testnet faucet when the account is new, or when the owner wants more test XRP; mainnet has none, so its account waits for the owner's deposit
Reports what the account holds, as its anchor proves it, for the wallet: XRP and its reserve, and each line with its freezes

Fakes the ledger for tests: XRP, trust lines, token payments through the issuer and their failures, issuers of DSUSD and RLUSD that mint, freeze and claw back, AMM pools that Payments with a `SendMax` swap through, and signer lists, regular keys and destination tags, with who may sign checked again as a transaction applies

Gives each fake ledger a real header and real hash trees of its transactions and its state, in rippled's binary form, pinned by objects captured from mainnet; validators that sign it, under a list their publisher signs; and the proof methods a patched rippled serves

Lies on request, in each way a server can lie to a node that checks the validators: made-up transactions, balances and absences, the branch of another key, old anchors, forged, replayed or withheld validations, a header that hashes wrong, a skip list of another chain, history left out, refusals and a made-up reset; over HTTPS too, beside its faucet, where its validators also rotate keys, sign nothing or publish a list on request

settlement.name: dassie-settlement
settlement.label: when & how to settle
settlement.desc: Where real-world ledgers plug in. A settlement scheme moves actual money through an external asset the node holds, such as an account on a ledger, and this crate decides when that is due.
does: The scheme interface, and when a scheme is active
A scheme that pauses, as a dollar token's off its peg: it settles nothing, cannot be paid and converts nothing meanwhile, and says why

External assets: what the node holds outside its books, as the ledger says, such as its accounts on the XRP Ledger and in settlement hubs, the testnet's and mainnet's kinds apart, apart from the schemes that settle through it, the documents they fetch through the node, such as validator lists, and what they wait for
Gas: a holding one scheme spends and another settles in is spent only within the owner's funds

The stub scheme, only in builds with debug assertions (dev, tests, simulations), never a release: 100 test USD, so everything works without a real ledger, in two kinds that peer only with their own: with commitments, peerings over a settlement hub without a hub, for tests of settlement; with unlimited trust, also what an empty config gives, peers that never settle, for every other test

The settlement policy: when a creditor asks a peer to settle, and how much the debtor pays, counted in the largest packet; credit over a hub is the member's hold toward its peer, and the default credit sizes what one request to settle funds it by; and the floor and the ceiling a node keeps its settlement hub account between
The owner's payments: a scheme pays the owner's funds out of its account, as the node moves them between two of its ledgers
Owner books: every XRP Ledger scheme, which the node never peers on, keeps what the node holds on its ledger and pays the owner's payments
Promises per packet, for schemes whose peerings carry them, as a settlement hub's do, and assets that talk to several endpoints, such as a hub's validators
Reconciling settlements still pending after a restart

hub.name: dassie-hub
hub.label: settlement hubs
hub.desc: A settlement hub lets two nodes peer without being able to walk away with what they owe each other: a small ledger kept by a few validators and backed by an escrow on the XRP Ledger, in XRP or in a token such as DSUSD. A payer sets funds aside in a hold, and its payee takes from it with the payer's signed promises.
does: The hub's rules, whose digest names the hub, and each validator's signed acceptance; the rules name the version of the hub protocol the hub runs, so validators on different releases never execute it differently, and the asset it holds, XRP or a token of an issuer; golden vectors pin the protocol of each version
Simplex consensus: an ordered log kept by a few validators, final in three message delays, with evidence that names whoever signed two histories
The ledger: accounts, holds, deposits and withdrawals, every table bounded, every drop accounted for after each block; each account counts what deposits credited it and what withdrawals took
Taking from a hold with the payer's claim, or with fulfilled commitments when the claim does not come, never twice
Fees split among the validators whose votes the log recorded
A validator's state as bytes, its consensus state and its ledger, from which it comes back after a restart without ever signing a vote that conflicts with one it sent
Test network resets written off in place

A token issuer's acts, as a quorum of validators attests them: a freeze or a transfer fee freezes the hub, which then takes only claims of packets in flight and lets no notice run until the thaw; a clawback ends it, and the payout set pays the withdrawals already on their way first and every account its share of what is left
Founding a hub: the sponsor's proposal, each validator's decision to accept or sign, and the genesis certificate, a quorum's signatures over the genesis block

The escrow on the XRP Ledger: the validators' keys, the sponsor's setup step by step and its check, for a token hub with its one trust line to the issuer and its fees paid in the escrow's own XRP, withdrawals, and the payout set that pays everyone out at the end, which each validator signs and hands to members a page at a time, and which a quorum's bundles put together

A validator's service, without IO: consensus and the ledger together, a bounded pool of operations with room kept for deadlines, the escrow's signatures gathered from the validators' keys only, and snapshots of the state checked against a certified root; it signs and submits nothing to an escrow the issuer holds, signs the payout set only once a block shows the thaw, or, for a hub that stopped while frozen, once its host proves the thaw, and attests again the deposits a freeze left without room; a token hub's validators end every answer to a member with the issuer's hold
What members and validators say to each other: requests, and statements a validator signs alone, which a member trusts once f + 1 validators signed them alike

A member's side: its account in the hub, which trusts what enough validators sign alike and reads the log in order, and the scheme on it that the hub's network and asset name, `hub-xrpl-testnet-xrp` or `hub-xrpl-testnet-dsusd` on the testnet, `hub-xrpl-xrp` or `hub-xrpl-rlusd` on mainnet, which funds holds, runs without an account of its own, advertised with none, until a peer's `pay` opens it, pays a peer without an account in with what it owes once that reaches the hub's minimum for a new account, leaves a redeem's fee in the account with every settlement, signs and checks the promises each packet carries, claims on the hub what its peer's claims leave out, withdraws for the owner, and books the owner's deposits and withdrawals from the account's counts

A member follows a token hub's freeze, keeping what waits for the thaw and claiming what the hub still pays: it reads the freeze from the issuer's hold f + 1 validators state, and the hub's method is unavailable until the thaw
The least XRP a token hub's escrow keeps for its fees, which a member checks, proven, and tops up before it asks for a withdrawal

The testnet's default hubs, of XRP and of DSUSD, each built in once founded under the current rules, with its keys at paths that name its network: boot1–4 its validators, founded by boot1, its escrow on the XRP Ledger testnet; a node joins one when its owner adds its scheme without naming another

Places for the default mainnet hubs, of XRP and of RLUSD, empty until the project's mainnet validators found them, and the default list of mainnet validators beside them; a test checks a built-in mainnet hub: its rules check, it holds its scheme's asset on mainnet, and every one of its validators is on the list

A member judges its hub failed once the hub refuses an operation for its shutdown, or f + 1 validators keep naming the same final block for as long as the hub's stall while fewer than f + 1 name a newer one: its scheme then can no longer receive, and the node drops the hub's methods; a freeze is no failure
Validators find the escrow's transactions by walking the history its proven state names, stepping through the proofs of the server's hints, and name the issuer's hold by the ledger it changed in

peer.name: dassie-peer
peer.label: node-to-node protocol
peer.desc: Peer protocol v1: how Dassie nodes find each other, peer and stay in sync.
does: The wire format and message authentication
The node table, link-state flooding, membership by majority and registration
Link states that say whether a node is a periphery node, where a core node's rate feed is, and which settlement hubs a node is in, each with the scheme it settles on there
Peering on its own, and routing, keeping a few first hops per node, picked by a hash only the node itself can compute

Periphery nodes without a URL and with no neighbors in their link state, which peer only with core nodes as their downlinks, and only with those their owner pinned when it pinned any, as many as a market maker trades through
Downlinks that never paid the node take at most half of its places for downlinks, so keys made for nothing cannot keep out those that pay
Advertising only peers that are alive and not stuck short of room, or being wound down, on every method, never ending one for room it could not pay
Delivering settlements and requests to settle, ending peerings, bans

Winding a settlement method down as a peering ends, on that method alone: no new packets from the peer on it, the peer asked to settle on it once, each step bounded, then the method dropped and the peer told, what is left staying owed; a method whose scheme the node no longer runs, or would settle directly on, as one a peering stored from when the XRP Ledger's schemes peered still has, or that has not been able to receive for as long as a silent peer is kept, is dropped at once; a peering left with no method ends
Settlement channels that close once idle, kept on disk so a late settlement still counts once

Settlement methods: a peering can hold a method for every hub both nodes are in, each agreed, added and dropped on its own, and every Prepare travels on one, over a hub with the payer's commitment, the payer's claim coming back in the reply to its Fulfill

Names people can say, at the bootstrap nodes as registrars: a log of sealed commitments, each name granted to the earliest one unsealed once every earlier window has closed, renewed by its holder, and a name list served as the node list is

Every node takes as a name's holder the node that more than two thirds of the registrars list, so one registrar that shows nodes different lists cannot give a name two holders, and keeps what it had while too few lists are fresh; a registrar releases a name that the others' lists show split

A registrant for the node's own names: the registration and its salt on disk before its sealed commitment goes to every registrar at once, the name unsealed only with every receipt and while the window allows, and renewed before it expires, in a registrar's grace period too

connector.name: dassie-connector
connector.label: routes ILP packets
connector.desc: The Interledger connector. A packet comes in from an endpoint; the connector picks a route, reserves the amount in the ledger, and settles the outcome when the answer comes back.
does: Endpoints: BTP clients, the local STREAM receiver, ILDCP
One endpoint per peer, with a slot for each settlement method of the peering: its ledger and account, its money in flight, and whether it is over a hub and available

Peers and the route table, with each packet's next hop drawn at random among a route's first hops with a method on the ledger it came in on, weighted by the fees each earned the node on that ledger, and a share of the draws even, so no one node can stop a payment; a packet goes on that method, or, where no hop has one, on the drawn hop's method with the best rate, and never moves to another method for room
Downlinks at child addresses below the node's own; a periphery node's addresses beneath its uplinks, forwarding nothing
A cap on money in flight on each method of a peer, which bounds what a crash loses, and no new packets from a peer it cannot answer

Exchange between currencies, with fees and a spread, at a rate moved from spot by what the owner holds on each ledger once the packet and those in flight have moved it, so that payments bring a skewed node back toward balance and no round trip gains, and nothing to or from a ledger whose scheme is paused

The same pricing on every ledger with a currency, a settlement hub's as much as an owner book's, and, for a packet that cannot keep its ledger, a ranking of the ledgers it could convert to by what it gets there relative to spot
A spending cap per BTP token
A packet trace for the debug pages
Waiting for a settlement hub's decision before rejecting a packet that went to a peer on a method over the hub

release-crate.name: dassie-release
release-crate.label: trusting a release
release-crate.desc: What a release is and how to trust one: versions, the mirror's layout, `SHA256SUMS` and its minisign signature. The updater and the release workflow both trust a release through it.
does: Versions that are safe as directory names
Moves on its own only to a later release
Checks minisign signatures strictly; the signature must name the version
Reads `SHA256SUMS` only once it is verified, with every parser bounded
Unpacks only plain files under `dassie/`

payments.name: dassie-payments
payments.label: Open Payments
payments.desc: Open Payments without IO: wallet addresses and their resources, GNAP grants, HTTP message signatures, payment pointers. The node serves it over HTTPS.
does: HTTP message signatures (RFC 9421) and content digests (RFC 9530), and the node's signature on its answers, which Dassie-aware clients check against the node ID
GNAP grant requests, access rules and the interaction hash
Wallet addresses, incoming payments, quotes and outgoing payments
Repeating intervals for grant limits
Payment pointers and recipients, for Send
Reads no clock, touches no network, and needs only `dassie-identity` of the other Dassie crates

ledger.name: dassie-ledger
ledger.label: double-entry books
ledger.desc: The node's books. Every transfer has two sides, every account has limits, and every change is written to a journal.
does: Accounts with credit and debit limits
Pending, committed and rolled-back transfers
What each token spent, read from the journal, for spending caps
The owner's group takes in what the node gains or loses
Property tests: no transfer breaks a limit, and balances always equal the journal
A closed list of ledgers, each named for its scheme and asset: each XRP Ledger network's XRP and dollar token, and each settlement hub's, the testnet's of test money and mainnet's of real money

node-core.name: dassie-node-core
node-core.label: the node's decisions
node-core.desc: Every decision the node makes, with no IO at all. Each is a function of its inputs, the time and an injected random source, so tests can replay it exactly.
does: Checking the config and the setup, and the realm: `live` is refused unless a dev switch that only builds with debug assertions honour allows it
Login, how long sessions last, and the same-origin rule
Rate limits
When to renew the TLS certificate

sim.name: dassie-sim
sim.label: runs simulations
sim.desc: A developer tool that runs the simulations from any seed, and the engine of the simulation campaign. Each simulation lives in the crate it simulates, and a seed fixes its whole run, so a seed that fails replays the same way every time.
does: Runs one seed, a range of seeds on every core, or the seed a git commit names: `dassie-sim run peer 0..1000`
Prints a run's trace to explain a failure: `dassie-sim explain peer 42`
Runs random seeds on every core as a campaign, mostly of the `node` simulation, and prints each run as a line of JSON: `dassie-sim campaign --minutes 60`
Gives each failure a signature, its simulation, outcome and the check or line that failed, the same for every seed that fails there
Tells a broken safety property from a network that never settled down
Runs a tripwire that fails on purpose now and then, so a campaign that stops shows
Builds with assertions on (`--profile sim`), so every invariant is checked as in tests

stream.name: dassie-stream
stream.label: STREAM payments
stream.desc: STREAM (Interledger RFC 29) sends money and data in many small ILP packets. Here it is a state machine: inputs go in, packets and timers come out.
does: Connections and a server, packet sizing, exchange-rate probing
Encryption as the RFC specifies; reads the deprecated receipts, never issues them
A limit on admission and on money per connection, and a cap on what a stream delivers
Byte-compatible with `ilp-protocol-stream`
Builds to WebAssembly

feed.name: dassie-feed
feed.label: the signed rate feed
feed.desc: The public feed in which a core node says what it converts at, so that market makers can trade through it. A feed is one signed UDP datagram, made once and sent to every subscriber.
does: The datagrams: subscribe, challenge and the signed feed, each within one packet
Cookies that prove a subscriber receives at its address, so a forged address never gets a feed
A subscriber table bounded in all and per client
When to publish: soon after the rates change, but never too often, and a heartbeat otherwise
A subscriber's side: verifies each feed and keeps only newer ones

identity.name: dassie-identity
identity.label: phrase → keys, node ID
identity.desc: Turns the owner's 20-word phrase into everything that identifies a node. The phrase names its realm and corrects a few wrong or unreadable words, never without the owner's say. The same phrase always gives the same node.
does: Phrases of 20 words with a realm, a creation time and Reed–Solomon check words, and every secret below the node key as one typed path: the login, ledger accounts, a hub's keys, STREAM receivers, QUIC keys
The Ed25519 node key, node ID and login secret
The node ID: 39 characters of base32, the same in ILP addresses, DNS names and the wallet, and 24 bytes on the wire
Signature checks under the ZIP-215 rules
Builds to WebAssembly

ilp.name: dassie-ilp
ilp.label: ILPv4 & BTP packets
ilp.desc: The Interledger packet formats. Encoders can write a header in place, so a packet is built without copying.
does: ILPv4 prepare, fulfill and reject
Addresses, timestamps and error codes
ILDCP: how a client learns its ILP address
BTP 2.0 framing
Builds to WebAssembly

base64url.name: dassie-base64url
base64url.label: strict base64url for IDs and tokens
base64url.desc: The text encoding of node IDs, the node's tokens and STREAM's connection tokens. It accepts only the canonical form, so an ID or a token cannot be written two ways.
does: Unpadded base64url (RFC 4648 §5), without allocating
Rejects padding, other alphabets and stray bits
Never panics on what it decodes

oer.name: dassie-oer
oer.label: canonical binary encoding (X.696 OER): every wire format above is written in it
oer.desc: The binary encoding all of Dassie's protocols use. It accepts only the canonical form, so each value has exactly one encoding.
does: Encoders, and decoders that do not copy
Rejects any non-canonical input
Property tests: round trips, and no panic on any bytes

kit.name: dassie-kit
kit.label: time units, client keys, the simulation kit
kit.desc: What the crates share below every protocol: units of time, the key that bounds requests per client, and the kit every simulation runs on. It depends on nothing of the workspace, so a protocol crate takes on nothing of the node's.
does: Seconds, minutes, hours and days in milliseconds
Who a request comes from: an IPv4 address or an IPv6 /56
A seeded random generator, how a simulated run ended, and running a range of seeds (`sim` feature)

steps.text: The owner opens the wallet, which the node serves from inside the dassie binary, and types the 20-word phrase. A phrase of the other realm is refused, and a corrected one is used only once the owner confirms it.
The browser derives the node key and a login proof with the node's own Rust code, compiled to WebAssembly. The phrase never leaves the browser.
The wallet sends only the proof over HTTPS. The node checks it and sets a session cookie.
Whether the proof is accepted, how long the session lasts, the same-origin rule and the rate limit are all decided here, without IO.
The wallet opens an RPC WebSocket and subscribes to live data such as ledgers, peers and logs.
Shared components show the first snapshot and keep it current as changes stream in.

flows.title: A BTP client pays the node

steps.text: An ILP client such as `ilp-plugin-btp` connects to the node's BTP server with a token the owner made in the wallet.
Each ILP Prepare packet is decoded. Only canonical encodings are accepted.
The connector checks the token's spending cap, finds the route, here the node's own STREAM receiver, and reserves the amount.
The ledger records a pending transfer in its journal.
The STREAM receiver decrypts the packet, credits the money and answers with a Fulfill.
The transfer commits. The money is held on one of the owner's ledgers, each backed by a settlement scheme.

flows.title: The owner sends to another wallet

steps.text: The owner enters a payment pointer or a payment request on the Send page.
The wallet asks the node over RPC for a quote, and then to pay.
The node finds the recipient, signs its requests, and creates an incoming payment and a quote on the other wallet, all through Open Payments.
STREAM sends the money in packets, which the connector routes across peers, each packet on a settlement method of the ledger the payment is made in where the next peer has one.
Each node books the Fulfill in its own books at once, and keeps it there whether or not its upstream peer counts it too.
The payment status page follows the outgoing payment live until it completes.
Nodes learn about each other from bootstrap nodes, agree on membership and peer on their own, exchanging signed messages.
Those messages travel over QUIC, one connection per pair of nodes, on UDP at each node's address.
Link state gives every node a route table, so packets are forwarded hop by hop across peers.

Each node's credit to the other is its own hold toward it in a hub they share, set aside so the other is paid whatever it does; it starts at nothing, so a payer funds its hold before its packets flow. Balances shift as packets flow.

Each hub two peers share is a settlement method of their peering, with its own credit on its own ledger. Once a peer comes close to the credit a node extends to it on a method, the node asks it to settle on that method, and the peer funds its hold toward the node in that hub, such as the XRP or DSUSD hub on the XRP Ledger testnet, from its owner's book there.
The settlement reaches the peer exactly once, even across crashes and restarts. Simulations check this for every seed.

When the owner removes a hub's scheme, the node settles up on that method first: it takes no new packets there, asks the peer to settle once, then drops the method within a few minutes. The scheme itself goes once the packets still in flight on that method have ended and what the peer may still have sent on it has had time to arrive. The peering carries on over their other hubs.
Once a day, a systemd timer runs `dassie update`.
It fetches the newest release's signed `SHA256SUMS` from get.dassie.land.
The signature and the version are checked before anything is unpacked, and the node moves only forward.
The new version starts. If it does not come up, the node goes back to the old one, with its data as the old one left it.

flows.button: A developer runs the dev network
flows.title: A developer runs the dev network

steps.text: `node --run dev` builds the dassie binary and the fake XRP Ledger, and starts one node per scenario on `dN.localhost`, behind an SNI proxy.
Each node is a real daemon with its own database, restarted when the Rust code changes.
The dev server sets the nodes up through their own RPC over the IPC socket, with the scenario code the end-to-end tests use.
The dashboard talks to the dev server on one origin and reaches each node through a relay.
The logs, the network graph and each node's debug pages use the same components as the wallet.

flows.button: A client reaches a node at home
flows.title: An Open Payments client reaches a node without a public address

steps.text: A node without a hostname keeps a QUIC connection open to the `dassiepay.net` front door, its relay unless it names another, from behind its NAT: over UDP, or where UDP is blocked, over a WebSocket to `relay.dassiepay.net/quic`.

A client asks for `https://<node ID>.dassiepay.net/.well-known/pay`. The front door reads the node ID from the host. Under a name, `https://<name>.dassiepay.net`, it takes the node a quorum of the bootstrap nodes' name lists names as the holder, reading those lists itself as every node does.
The front door opens a relayed stream on the node's connection, runs TLS inside it pinned to the node's key, and passes the request on with its name unchanged.
The node answers under that name and signs the answer with its node key.

The front door passes the JSON back unchanged. A Dassie-aware client checks the signature against the node the host names, or the name's holder in its own view; any other client trusts the front door.

flows.button: A market maker rebalances a node
flows.title: A market maker brings a core node back toward balance

steps.text: A core node in an XRP hub and a dollar token's hub converts between the two hubs' ledgers, and prices each conversion by what it holds: short of dollars, it takes them in at better than its spot rate, and gives them out at worse. This needs it to count each asset whole, a hub's ledger together with the owner book that funds it; for now it prices each ledger apart, which can send trades the other way.
It publishes those rates as one signed UDP datagram, sent to every subscriber that proved its address with a cookie.

`dassie market-maker` verifies the feed against the node's key from its discovery document, as it does for each core node it trades through, and reads the XRP Ledger's AMM pool with `amm_info`. This node pays more for dollars than the pool and the others do, by more than the market maker's margin.

The market maker runs two periphery nodes, one in each hub, each pinned to every core node it trades through and peered with it over the hub they share. Over their IPC sockets, one creates an incoming payment on its hub's ledger beneath this core node, and the other quotes paying it a fixed amount from its own hub, and pays only if the quote still clears the margin.

STREAM carries the dollars to the core node over the dollar hub, which converts them to XRP at its curve's rate and passes them on over the XRP hub. Each pair of nodes settles over the hub it shares, and each node moves funds between its hub and its owner book by itself.

Once the XRP node holds more than its band, in its hub and its owner book together, the market maker swaps the surplus back into dollars through the pool: one Payment from that node's owner book's account to the other's, whose `SendMax` bounds the price. Once the core node prices each asset whole, it holds more dollars than before, and the market maker more value.

flows.title: An owner registers a name for their node

steps.text: On the wallet's Names page, the owner asks for a name. The node checks that it is one, and that no registrar's fresh list names anyone for it.
The node draws a salt and writes the registration to its database, and only then sends the sealed commitment, a hash of the name, its node ID and the salt, to every bootstrap node at once.
Each bootstrap node, a registrar, logs the commitment at the next place in its log, writes it to disk and answers with a receipt. None of them learns the name.

With every receipt in hand, and time left in the window, the node sends each registrar the name and the salt. Each registrar grants the name to the commitment it logged first, once that commitment's window closes, and lists it.

Every node reads the registrars' name lists and takes as the holder the node that more than two thirds of them list. The wallet shows the name as the owner's, and the node renews it before it expires.

The node now accepts Open Payments requests under `<name>.dassiepay.net` as well, and signs every answer. The front door reads the registrars' lists too, and passes requests under the name to the node. Another Dassie node paying it there takes an answer only if the holder its own view names signed it.

testsIntro: Confidence comes mainly from deterministic simulation. The cores never read a clock or the system's random generator, so a whole network of nodes runs in one process from a seed: the same seed gives the same run. The other kinds of test pin down what a simulation cannot judge.

tests.p: Whole networks run in one process with a fake clock and a seeded random generator, at the timings of a real node: a simulated day takes seconds. Faults are injected: latency, loss, a forger that sends copies of requests as its own, clocks that are off, crashes, mid-payment too, commits that fail, restarts, and partitions, some longer than a day, and owners end peerings and ban peers. Every state machine checks its invariants after each step, and a failure prints the seed that reproduces it. A node run draws its whole network, its faults and its payments from the seed, and once healed must settle down. Scripted node runs keep each node's owner books on a fake XRP Ledger, XRP and DSUSD on its testnet and, in the live realm, XRP and RLUSD on its mainnet, whose issuers freeze lines and claw back while owners pay out, and each node is judged by its own books. On the fake ledger, servers lie to the nodes, each kind of lie in turn in a scripted run, and validators rotate keys, withhold a quorum and let a list lapse: no node may book, cancel or write off anything the ledger did not do, and each counts what it proved, so a run shows that it went through the checks of the validators. One runs nodes peered over a settlement hub whose validators, some of them faulty, run in the same process, with a member that lies about its claims, until the hub stalls and its escrow on the fake ledger pays everyone out. Over such a hub, servers also lie to its members and its validators, each kind of lie in turn, while they pay and move funds into it; nodes pay across dollars held in a DSUSD hub and XRP held in an XRP hub, through nodes in both that convert between them; and nodes in both hubs peer over both; an owner removes one hub's scheme, whose methods wind down while the peerings carry on, and when that hub fails and pays out, its members stop receiving over it and the other hub carries their payments on. Among five nodes in both hubs, payments keep their ledger without converting, each packet's next hop is drawn by the fees each earned, and a hop short of room answers T04 and keeps its weight. Members of a DSUSD hub send nothing over it while its issuer freezes it and pay again after the thaw, top up its escrow's XRP before a withdrawal, and are paid out in DSUSD, pro rata after a clawback; a newcomer with no account in a hub is paid into it by a member it peers with. The hubs' validators follow their escrows through proofs, while their servers lie too. In the live realm, members of an XRP hub and of an RLUSD hub on the fake ledger's mainnet, which each run founds, fund them from their owner books and pay each other over them while their servers and the validators' lie, and RLUSD's pool moved off its peg halts conversions while they still pay over it. Node runs not about settlement run on a stub with unlimited trust, and runs about settlement on a stub with commitments or a simulated hub; no test settles directly. Another has nodes register names with four bootstrap nodes, one of which may show nodes different name lists, hold back receipts, or tell a front-runner every name unsealed at it, and checks that no two nodes ever take different holders for a name and that the front-runner never holds one. Tests run each scripted situation on one fixed seed, and the `node` simulation's fixed seeds include one over a settlement hub, and the lying servers over a hub must tell every kind of lie; the drawn runs are the campaign's, and `dassie-sim` runs any seed.
tests.ev: src/sim in dassie-stream, dassie-connector, dassie-peer, dassie-hub and dassie-node, run by their tests and by dassie-sim

tests.p: Outside CI, spot VMs run the simulations from random seeds, loop after loop: mostly `main`, and pull requests labelled `sim`. Each kind of failure becomes one GitHub issue with the seed that reproduces it, and a pull request's become comments on it. The campaign is not a CI check: it posts no commit status. When the campaign cannot build `main` itself, it says so in an issue of its own rather than going quiet. A pull request's code builds and runs in a sandbox with no network and nothing secret to read.

Byte-exact fixtures from other implementations: Dassie's first, TypeScript one, `xrpl.js`, and for every key a node derives from its phrase, a generator apart from Dassie's code. They pin the wire formats and key derivations.
Random inputs: round trips, canonical-only parsing, decoders that never panic, ledger balances that always equal the journal, spending caps.
Dassie talks to independent implementations: the npm `ilp-protocol-stream` both ways, from native code and from WebAssembly, and in a browser.

Real binaries and real sockets: a fresh install, payments and settlement across nodes and across two hubs, mainnet's schemes in the live realm on the fake ledger, nodes that book nothing while its server lies, Open Payments, the wallet in a browser, and the installer and updater on four Linux distributions.

changes: The testnet's settlement hub runs, kept by the four bootstrap nodes as its validators, and is built in as the default hub. A node joins it when its owner adds the `hub-xrp-testnet` scheme, which the wallet now offers and describes: the node moves about 2.5 test XRP from its XRP Ledger testnet account into the hub, and then peers over the hub with other members of it.
Nothing changes for a node that doesn't add the scheme, and the peerings a node already has stay as they are.

A node can settle with its peers through a settlement hub: a small ledger kept by a few validators and backed by an escrow on the XRP Ledger testnet. Over a hub, a payer sets money aside in a hold toward its peer, and that hold is all the credit the peer extends, so neither side can walk away with what it owes. No hub runs on the testnet yet, so nothing changes for a node until one does, and the wallet doesn't offer the hub scheme until there is a default hub.

A node keeps its hub account funded from its XRP Ledger testnet account on its own, between a floor and a ceiling, and the owner can move money with `dassie hub deposit`, `dassie hub withdraw` and `dassie hub status`.

A node can run as one of a hub's validators: `DASSIE_VALIDATOR_CONFIG` names the sponsors it agrees to found hubs with, and `dassie hub found` founds a hub with validators that agreed, and sets up its escrow.
The testnet's bootstrap nodes now all run in us-east1, and a fourth, boot4.dassie.xyz, joins the default list.
A node no longer aborts when a QUIC stream is read first in order and then out of order, a bug in quinn-proto that the market maker's node ran into.
Open Payments grants approved earlier with a limit on what is received but none on what is debited are revoked, since nothing bounded what they could debit.

A market maker's periphery node may keep up to 128 uplinks: list them in `DASSIE_UPLINKS`. A periphery node's self-description to its uplinks no longer lists them as neighbors, since only core nodes have neighbors.

`dassie market-maker` trades through several core nodes with its same two nodes. It follows each one's feed and takes the best trade each time, and its VM trades through boot1, boot2 and boot3 by default.
An incoming payment on a periphery node can be received beneath a chosen uplink, with `uplink` in the owner's `CreateIncomingPayment`.

A settlement channel with a node the node no longer peers with closes after a day idle, once nothing of it is pending. Its place is freed for new peers, and its accounts and sequences stay, so peering again carries on where it left off.
An Open Payments grant may limit what is debited and what is received together, but no longer what is received alone, and a receive limit now caps what payments actually deliver.
The groundwork for settlement hubs is in the code. No hub runs yet, and nothing changes for a node until one does.

A node's STREAM receiver never lowers the most it has told a sender it may send, as the STREAM specification asks. When several payments race into one incoming payment, payments that fit together all complete. A payment the receiver can no longer take is told the receiver takes no more, and closed, rather than refused until its deadline. A Dassie payment that is short by no more than its tolerance then counts as complete.

`dassie market-maker` no longer stalls when one of its nodes is above its band and the other has no room: it trades from the node with no room into the one above its band, which makes room, and then rebalances. The market maker's VM now leaves room for all the XRP the testnet faucet grants.
`tokio` is updated, for advisory RUSTSEC-2026-0386.

`dassie setup --passphrase-file <file>` sets a node up from its recovery phrase without a browser, for a headless node or a market maker's own nodes. It sends the node key only to the node's own certificate, which the node names over its owner socket, and it can add settlement schemes with `--scheme`. Running it again changes nothing.
A constant-time helper the cryptography libraries use is updated, for advisory RUSTSEC-2026-0385.

A core node prices what it converts by what it holds. When it runs short of one asset, it pays a little more for that asset and asks more for it, so trading brings it back. The new rebalancing setting beside the spread says how strongly, 5% by default, and each packet pays for its own effect on the price.

A core node publishes the rates it converts at as a signed feed on UDP port 7768, from the new `dassie-feed.socket`, to subscribers that first prove their address. `GET /stats` and the node's link state name the port. An update turns the socket on, so open UDP 7768 in your firewall for subscribers to reach the feed; on NixOS, `openFirewall` now opens it.

`dassie market-maker` trades through a node when the node's feed and an AMM pool on the XRP Ledger leave a margin, then swaps its funds back through the pool. It trades through two periphery nodes of your own, each pinned to the node with the new `DASSIE_UPLINKS`, and signs only for the XRP Ledger testnet.

A new settlement scheme, `xrpl-testnet-dsusd`, settles in DSUSD, Dassie's own testnet dollar, beside RLUSD. There is no DSUSD faucet: buy it with XRP through the testnet's XRP/DSUSD pool, which is kept at the market's XRP price.
The owner's Send also pays STREAM credentials, an ILP address and a shared secret.
A payment no longer fails at its very end when the receiver's answers arrive out of order.

Opening a node's front door name, `https://<node ID>.dassiepay.net/`, in a browser shows a short page the front door writes itself: the node ID the name stands for, whether that node is connected now, and its wallet address. The page runs no script and sets no cookie.
The wallet's Settings lists paired devices, with a Revoke for each, and pairs a new one with a QR code. It also shows which version of Dassie the node runs.
A new node with a single bootstrap node always finds its first peers: while it has none, it also asks the bootstrap node for its own link state.

Payments finish more reliably when the incoming payment being paid into has less room left than a packet, as when two payers share one: the sender sends what fits, a receiver without room is asked again, and a closed connection keeps saying why it closed.

An incoming payment counts as paid once it is within a ten-thousandth of a unit of its amount, under or over, since rounding along the path keeps a payment from landing exactly. Its `receivedAmount` in Open Payments can therefore exceed its `incomingAmount` by that much.

A node can settle in RLUSD, Ripple's dollar token, on the XRP Ledger testnet, with the `xrpl-testnet-rlusd` scheme. It shares the node's XRPL account with `xrpl-testnet`: the node sets up its RLUSD trust line itself, pays the fees in XRP, and books RLUSD as dollars. Test RLUSD comes from Ripple's faucet at tryrlusd.com.

The wallet has a page of external assets, showing what the node's XRPL account holds as the ledger reports it: XRP, RLUSD, the reserve, and whether the issuer has frozen the line. Receive says where to send XRP, with the testnet faucet, and RLUSD.

While RLUSD's issuer freezes the node's line, the node settles nothing on it. While the issuer deep-freezes the line, freezes RLUSD for every holder, or charges a transfer fee, the node also asks no peer to pay into it, and no peer is cut off for what it could not pay.
On NixOS, each release comes as a flake: point a flake input at `https://get.dassie.land/flake/latest.tar.gz` and enable `services.dassie`. It runs the release's signed binary, with no updater.
A node holds a lock on its data directory, so a second daemon on the same directory refuses to start.
A node whose Fulfill is refused because its clock is behind a peer that just restarted sends it again, so the two nodes' books no longer drift apart from this and stall payments between them.

A node without a hostname keeps a connection to the dassiepay.net front door by default, so Open Payments clients reach it at `<node ID>.dassiepay.net` with no setup. The front door, which the project runs, then sees when such a node is online. Set `DASSIE_RELAY` to another relay, or to nothing to keep none.

`dassie status` describes a periphery node as one: its uplinks, its relay and whether it is connected, and the names it answers to. The wallet says whether its front door can reach the node right now.
The log says at startup whether the node has QUIC, and which transport each peer is reached over.

Downlinks and core peers have QUIC connection places of their own, so a crowd of periphery nodes or strangers cannot crowd out a node's core links. A node with no room left says so, and the asking node turns to HTTPS.

The consent page says what is sent, what is received and for how long, and warns of a receive limit no payment can fit. A payer tells a receiver that stopped a payment early from one that received all of it.

Peers talk over QUIC on UDP port 443, each checking the other's node key instead of a certificate authority; a peer that cannot be reached over UDP is asked over HTTPS. Installs gain a `dassie-quic.socket` unit, which the updater turns on.
A node without a hostname joins as a periphery node: it peers with core nodes as their downlink, keeps its connections to them open, and is paid at an address beneath each of them.
Any node relays encrypted streams to the nodes connected to it, and a node can keep a connection to a relay of its choice with `DASSIE_RELAY`.

Open Payments answers are signed with the node's key. A node without a hostname answers under `<node ID>.dassiepay.net` and the names in `DASSIE_PUBLIC_NAMES`, and `dassie front-door` runs a front door that passes Open Payments requests on to such nodes.
Ending a peering collects what the peer owes first and settles nothing for the end, a peer that stays short of room is set apart, and a ban takes effect at once.

Hardening and fixes: XRP Ledger settlement copes with servers that lag or forget history, the updater keeps a node stopped when its database cannot be put back, and skips a version it rolled back, the installer never runs beside an update, and limits hold for strangers' replays, probes and Open Payments clients.
The wallet's Network page draws the routing table, and lists peers that have gone offline apart from those still heard from.
A grant may limit what it debits or what it delivers, not both, as Open Payments asks; the wallet says which.
STREAM backs off once for a burst of rejected packets, so a payment that runs out of credit resumes in moments instead of tens of seconds.
The daily updater runs in a systemd sandbox, and the node's unit is tighter.

Hardening: another wallet's URL can no longer reach private addresses through an IPv6 literal, a bootstrap key of the wrong length is reported as an invalid `DASSIE_BOOTSTRAP_NODES` instead of crashing the node, far-apart exchange rates no longer stop the rate task, and every payment ID has one spelling.
A new node joins the public testnet on its own: its bootstrap nodes are boot1–boot3.dassie.xyz unless `DASSIE_BOOTSTRAP_NODES` names others.
The installer and the updater keep to the channel a node was installed from.
XRP Ledger settlement runs on the testnet only.
Connections share the node's slots fairly, and a BTP client that has gone away answers with an ILP Reject.
Hardening: the setup URL stays out of the journal, dev flags warn on a public listener, more non-public addresses are refused, and a revoked grant leaves the owner's connected apps.
Updates that fail roll back: if a new version does not start, the node goes back to the old one, with its data as the old one left it.
`dassie status` shows how a node is doing, and the setup URL survives restarts; `dassie setup-url` prints it again.
Let's Encrypt accepts the node's certificate requests again.
Open Payments: each payment gets a STREAM connection of its own, and each item of a grant keeps to its own limits.
The node checks its books and its state machines for consistency as it runs.
The first release of Dassie in Rust: one static binary for x64 and arm64 Linux, signed, installed with one command and updated every day.
A node finds peers on its own, routes Interledger payments across them, and settles with them on the XRP Ledger testnet.
Apps pay through it with Open Payments or BTP, and payments convert between currencies at fetched rates.
Each peer gets a grace limit, and a peer that costs more than that is banned.
The owner runs the node from a wallet it serves itself.
